tips.title: Radius, not diameter, in πr²
tips.body: Measure the clear zone's **diameter**, then **halve it** before squaring. Forgetting to halve makes the area four times too big, which is the single most common calculation error in this topic.

tips.title: Antibiotic against antiseptic
tips.body: **Antibiotics** are taken **inside** the body and kill bacteria. **Antiseptics** are used **outside**, on skin and surfaces. Neither works on a virus.

tips.title: Aseptic technique, and why each step
tips.body: Flame the loop, lift the lid at an angle, tape it partly shut. Each step stops other microorganisms getting in, so anything that grows is what you put there. Say the reason, not just the step.

tips.title: Halve the diameter once, at the start
tips.body: Zone-of-inhibition questions give a **diameter**, and the formula needs a **radius**. Write $r = d \div 2$ on its own line **before** you touch $\pi r^2$. Doing it first means it cannot be forgotten halfway through, which is where the mark usually goes.

why.matters:
Medicines are mostly not cures in the way people imagine. A painkiller treats the symptom and leaves the cause; an antibiotic kills the bacterium and does nothing to a virus; and most of what a hospital does is help the body do its own work.

What this topic is really about is how we know a drug works at all. A new medicine has to be shown to be **safe, effective and correctly dosed** before anybody takes it, and the trial design that establishes that is as much a part of the science as the chemistry of the drug.

examples.title: Why you finish the course
examples.body:
Stopping when you feel better leaves behind the bacteria that took longest to kill — which are, by definition, the ones least affected by the antibiotic. They are the ones that then multiply.

Resistance is not something an individual bacterium learns; it is **selection**. A population already varies, the antibiotic kills the susceptible ones, and what is left rebuilds the population from the survivors. Do that often enough — unfinished courses, antibiotics for viruses, antibiotics in farming — and the drug stops working for everybody.

visual.alt: A flow chart of antibiotic resistance as selection: a varied population is mostly killed by the antibiotic, the least affected bacteria survive and multiply, and the population that rebuilds is resistant

examples.title: Why a new drug takes years to arrive
examples.body:
A promising molecule is not a medicine. Before anyone can be given it, three questions have to be answered in order: is it **toxic**, does it **work**, and what is the right **dose**.

So it is tested on cells and tissues, then on animals, then on a small number of healthy volunteers, and only then on patients. The last stage is usually **double blind**: some patients get a **placebo**, and neither they nor the doctor knows who — because expecting to improve makes people report improvement, and a doctor who knows will treat the two groups differently without meaning to.

rows: is it safe, and at what dose?

visual.alt: A table of the stages of drug testing: preclinical work on cells, tissues and then animals, then healthy volunteers for safety and dose, and finally a double blind trial on patients to see whether it works

examples.title: Why a pregnancy test is a line that appears
examples.body:
A **monoclonal antibody** is made from one clone of cells, so every copy is identical and binds to exactly one target. That is the useful part: you can pick out one molecule from everything else in a sample.

A pregnancy test uses antibodies that bind only to the hormone **hCG**. If it is there, it is caught at a line of fixed antibodies and drags a coloured marker with it, so a line appears; if it is not, nothing sticks and nothing shows. The same specificity is why monoclonals are used to find one kind of cell in a sample and to carry a drug to it.

steps.title: Antibiotics work on bacteria, and only bacteria
steps.body:
An **antibiotic** is a medicine that kills bacteria or stops them growing. It works because it **stops a process inside the bacterial cell that the host's cells do not have**, or do differently: building the bacterial cell wall, for example, or making proteins with the bacterium's own ribosomes. So the bacteria are harmed and the person's cells are not.

A **virus** has no processes of its own to stop. It reproduces inside the host's cells, using the host's machinery. An antibiotic cannot touch it without harming the cell, which is why doctors do not give antibiotics for a cold or flu.

Do not confuse the words: **antibodies** are made by your lymphocytes; **antibiotics** are drugs.

steps.title: Aseptic technique: growing only what you mean to
steps.body:
*(Biology only.)* To test antibiotics in the lab, you first have to grow bacteria — and only the bacteria you want. **Aseptic technique** keeps other microorganisms out.

- **Sterilise** the growth medium (agar) and Petri dishes in an **autoclave**, which uses steam under high pressure to kill any microorganisms.
- **Flame the inoculating loop** until it glows red, then let it cool, so it carries only the bacteria you are transferring.
- **Work next to a lit Bunsen burner**: hot air rising from the flame carries airborne microorganisms up and away from the open dish.
- **Keep dishes and culture vials covered**, lifting the lid only a little and only when needed, so microorganisms from the air cannot land on the agar.

In school labs the lid is also taped at two points rather than sealed, and cultures are grown at about 25 °C rather than body temperature, so harmful pathogens that thrive at 37 °C are less likely to grow.

steps.title: Core practical: antiseptics, antibiotics or plant extracts
steps.body:
*(Biology only.)* This is core practical 5.18B. Bacteria are spread over an agar plate, discs soaked in different substances are placed on top, and after incubation each disc has a **clear zone** where the bacteria could not grow. The larger the clear zone, the better that substance is at stopping this bacterium.

**Sources of error.** Zone edges can be blurred or not circular, so measure two diameters at right angles and take the mean. Contamination shows up as colonies that look different from the rest. The substance may spread unevenly from the disc. Repeat each substance on more discs or plates and take a mean, so one odd zone does not decide the result.

steps.title: Calculating areas with πr²
steps.body: *(Biology only.)* Specification point 5.19B asks you to calculate the cross-sectional area of a bacterial culture, or of a clear zone, using **area = πr²**. You measure the **diameter** with a ruler, so the first step is always to **halve it**.

Area = πr² = π × 7²
= **153.9 mm²** (to 1 decimal place)

steps.title: From discovery to medicine
steps.body:
Developing a new medicine, including a new antibiotic, takes many years and has several stages.

1. **Discovery**: a substance that might work is found, for example in a plant or a microorganism, or designed from knowledge of the disease.
2. **Development**: it is made in a form that can be tested, and its likely dose is worked out.
3. **Preclinical testing**: tested on **cells and tissues** in the lab, then on **animals**, to check it works and is not **toxic**.
4. **Clinical testing**: tested on **people**. First small doses on healthy volunteers, to check it is safe; then on patients, to find the best dose and whether it works.

In the best clinical trials some patients get a **placebo** — a dummy with no drug — and the trial is **double-blind**: neither patients nor doctors know who has which, so expectations cannot affect the results.

steps.title: Making monoclonal antibodies
steps.body:
*(Higher tier, Biology only.)* A **monoclonal antibody** is one kind of antibody, made in large amounts, all identical, all complementary to the same antigen. The problem is that the lymphocytes which make a particular antibody **do not divide**, so you cannot grow many of them.

The answer is to combine two cells:
- a **lymphocyte** that makes the antibody you want (collected from a mouse given the antigen), which cannot divide;
- a **tumour cell**, which divides rapidly but makes no antibody.

Fused together they form a **hybridoma** cell. It divides again and again, and every copy makes the same antibody. That is where *monoclonal* comes from: antibodies from one clone of cells.

steps.text: A mouse is given the antigen, so it makes lymphocytes that produce the antibody
These lymphocytes make the right antibody but **cannot divide**
They are fused with **tumour cells**, which divide rapidly
The fused cell is a **hybridoma**
Hybridomas divide and make large amounts of identical antibody

check.prompt: What name is given to the cell made by fusing a lymphocyte with a tumour cell?
check.solution: A **hybridoma**. Fusing the two combines the lymphocyte's ability to make one specific antibody with the tumour cell's ability to divide indefinitely, so the cell both produces the antibody and multiplies.

markScheme.description: hybridoma

steps.title: What monoclonal antibodies are used for
steps.body:
*(Higher tier, Biology only.)* Because each monoclonal antibody binds to **one specific antigen**, it can find one particular molecule or cell in the body.

- **Pregnancy tests.** Urine of a pregnant woman contains the hormone **hCG**. Antibodies complementary to hCG, on coloured beads, bind to it; antibodies fixed on the strip then hold it, giving a coloured line.
- **Diagnosis.** Antibodies carrying a radioactive or fluorescent marker bind to **blood clots** or **cancer cells**, so a scan shows where they are.
- **Treatment.** Antibodies carrying a drug or radioactive substance bind to **cancer cells** and deliver it there, or mark the cells for the immune system to destroy.

The advantage over ordinary drugs and radiotherapy is **targeting**: the antibody goes only to the cells with that antigen, so fewer healthy cells are harmed and there are fewer side effects.

Notice that the diameters differ by a third, but the areas differ by much more. That is why the specification asks for areas: area grows with the **square** of the radius.

steps.title: Going deeper: say what the drug does, and why it targets
steps.body:
The top marks in this topic go to answers that say **why**, not just **what**.

**Antibiotics.** Not *antibiotics kill bacteria* but *antibiotics stop a process in bacterial cells, such as making the cell wall, that human cells do not have*. Then the unfamiliar question — a new drug that blocks something — becomes easy: does the human cell have that thing?

**The core practical.** Compare **areas**, use a **control disc**, and conclude only about *this* bacterium.

**Monoclonal antibodies.** Say what each cell brings to the hybridoma: the lymphocyte the antibody, the tumour cell division. For uses, always come back to **specific binding**: that is what makes a pregnancy test work and what makes cancer treatment targeted.

**Trials.** Explain *why* double-blind: expectations cannot affect the results.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Antibiotics** stop processes in bacterial cells that host cells lack, so they only treat **bacterial** infections — never viruses.
- **Aseptic technique**: autoclave the agar and dishes; flame and cool the loop; work next to a lit Bunsen burner; keep lids and vials covered.
- **Core practical 5.18B**: discs of each substance plus a sterile-water control on a lawn of bacteria; the bigger the **clear zone**, the more effective. Measure two diameters and take the mean; repeat.
- **Area = πr²**: halve the diameter first; clear agar = zone − disc.
- **New medicines**: discovery → development → preclinical (cells, tissues, animals) → clinical (volunteers, then patients); placebos and double-blind trials.
- **Monoclonal antibodies**: lymphocyte (antibody, no division) + tumour cell (divides) → **hybridoma** → many identical antibodies.
- **Uses**: pregnancy tests (hCG), locating clots and cancer cells, targeted cancer treatment with fewer side effects.

questions.prompt: A student spreads one type of bacterium on an agar plate. After incubation the plate has colonies of two different colours. Which mistake most likely caused this?
questions.skill: diagnosing a failure of aseptic technique
questions.solution: **The lid was left off, so microorganisms from the air landed on the agar.** A second colour means a second kind of microorganism is growing, so the culture is contaminated. Petri dishes are kept covered, and the lid is lifted as little as possible, precisely so that spores and bacteria in the air cannot fall onto the agar. Autoclaving kills microorganisms; it cannot create new ones. Flaming the loop sterilises it, which is the correct technique and would not change the colour of anything. Incubating at a different temperature changes how fast colonies grow, not what kind of organism they are.

markScheme.description: the lid was left off, so microorganisms from the air contaminated the agar

options: The agar was autoclaved for too long, which turned some of the agar into a second kind of bacterium
The lid was left off the dish for several minutes, so microorganisms from the air landed on the agar and grew
The inoculating loop was flamed before use, and the heat changed the colour of the bacteria it picked up
The dish was incubated at 20 °C rather than 25 °C, so some of the bacteria grew into a different colour

questions.prompt: To find a blood clot, doctors inject monoclonal antibodies carrying a radioactive marker. The antibodies bind to a protein found only in blood clots, and a scanner shows where the radioactivity collects. Why do the antibodies collect at the clot rather than throughout the body?
questions.solution: **Each monoclonal antibody is complementary to one specific antigen.** The antibodies were made to bind to a protein found only in clots, so wherever the blood carries them they bind only where that protein is, and the radioactive marker they carry builds up there. That is what makes monoclonal antibodies useful for locating clots and cancer cells: they find one particular molecule. The marker itself has no attraction to clots, antibodies are carried freely in the blood rather than being trapped by size, and they are made by hybridoma cells in a laboratory, not from the patient's clotting proteins.

markScheme.description: the antibody is complementary to an antigen found only on the clot, so it binds only there

options: Each monoclonal antibody is complementary to one specific antigen, and that antigen is found only in the clot
The radioactive marker is attracted to blood clots, and it drags the antibodies along with it to the clot
The antibodies are too large to travel past the clot, so they pile up against it wherever the blood is blocked
The antibodies are made from the patient's own clotting proteins, so they join the clot as it forms

questions.prompt: Name the type of cell that is fused with an antibody-producing lymphocyte to make a hybridoma.
questions.solution: **A tumour cell.** The lymphocyte produces the desired antibody but does not divide; the tumour cell divides rapidly but makes no useful antibody. Fused together they form a hybridoma, which both divides and produces the antibody.

markScheme.description: tumour cell (accept myeloma or cancer cell)

questions.prompt: A paper disc of diameter 6 mm, soaked in an antibiotic, is placed on an agar plate spread with bacteria. After incubation the clear zone, measured across and including the disc, has a diameter of 20 mm. Using area = πr², calculate the area of the clear agar around the disc, not counting the disc itself. Give your answer in mm² to 1 decimal place.
questions.solution: Halve each diameter first. Clear zone including the disc: $r = 10$ mm, area $= \pi \times 10^2 = 314.2$ mm². Disc: $r = 3$ mm, area $= \pi \times 3^2 = 28.3$ mm². Clear agar around the disc $= 314.2 - 28.3 = 285.9$ mm² (exactly, $\pi \times (100 - 9) = \pi \times 91 = 285.9$ mm²). The disc is subtracted because the bacteria could never have grown under it, so only the ring around it shows the antibiotic at work. Using the diameter as the radius is the common mistake: it gives an area four times too big.

markScheme.description: halves both diameters and finds both areas: 314.2 mm² and 28.3 mm²
285.9 mm² (accept 285.7 from π = 3.14)

questions.prompt: A Petri dish is filled with agar to a diameter of 90 mm and spread with bacteria. A single antibiotic disc is placed at the centre, and after incubation a circular clear zone of diameter 18 mm has formed around it. Using area = πr², calculate the percentage of the agar surface that is clear.
questions.skill: clear zone as a share of the plate
questions.solution: Radii first: the agar has $r = 45$ mm and the clear zone $r = 9$ mm. Area of agar $= \pi \times 45^2 = 6361.7$ mm². Area of clear zone $= \pi \times 9^2 = 254.5$ mm². Percentage clear $= \dfrac{254.5}{6361.7} \times 100 = 4$%. (Shortcut: π cancels, so the fraction is $\dfrac{9^2}{45^2} = \dfrac{81}{2025} = 0.04$.) The clear zone is where the antibiotic diffused far enough through the agar to stop the bacteria growing.

markScheme.description: halves both diameters to radii of 45 mm and 9 mm and finds both areas (6361.7 and 254.5 mm²)
divides the clear-zone area by the agar area and multiplies by 100

questions.prompt: Before bacteria are transferred to an agar plate, the inoculating loop is heated in a Bunsen flame and then allowed to cool for a few seconds before it touches the bacteria. Explain why both steps are needed.
questions.skill: aseptic technique with the inoculating loop
questions.solution: Heating the loop until it glows **sterilises** it, killing any microorganisms already on it, so the only thing transferred to the agar is the bacterium being studied. The loop must then **cool**, because a red-hot loop would **kill the bacteria** it is meant to pick up, and nothing would grow on the plate.

markScheme.description: flaming sterilises the loop so no other microorganisms are transferred
cooling stops the hot loop killing the bacteria being transferred

criteria.text: Explains that heating the loop in the flame sterilises it, killing any microorganisms on it so that only the intended bacteria are transferred
Explains that the loop is allowed to cool because a hot loop would kill the bacteria it is meant to pick up

questions.modelAnswer: Passing the loop through the flame until it glows red kills any microorganisms that were on it from the air or from the last time it was used. This sterilises the loop, so when it touches the agar it transfers only the bacterium being studied and the culture is not contaminated. The loop then has to cool for a few seconds, because metal straight out of a Bunsen flame is hot enough to kill bacteria on contact. If it touched the culture while still hot it would kill the very bacteria it is meant to transfer, and nothing would grow on the plate.

questions.prompt: A new antibiotic has passed preclinical testing on cells, tissues and animals. In the first clinical trials it is given to a small number of healthy volunteers, at a very low dose. Explain why the first human tests are done in this way.
questions.skill: the design of early clinical trials
questions.solution: Preclinical results show how the drug behaves in cells and in animals, not in the human body, so the first clinical trials are about **safety**: finding out whether the drug causes harmful side effects in people. **Healthy volunteers** are used so that any effect seen is the drug's and is not confused with the illness, and so that a sick patient is not put at risk by an untested drug. The dose starts **very low** and is raised gradually, because the amount that is safe and effective in a person is not yet known, and a low dose limits the harm if the drug turns out to be more toxic in humans than in animals.

markScheme.description: the first human tests check safety and side effects, which animal and cell tests cannot fully show
healthy volunteers so effects are not confused with illness and no sick patient is put at risk
a very low dose because the safe and effective dose in people is unknown, limiting harm if it is toxic

criteria.text: Explains that the first tests on people are about safety: whether the drug has harmful side effects in the human body, which tests on cells and animals cannot fully show
Explains that healthy volunteers are used so that any effect observed is caused by the drug rather than by an illness, and so that no sick patient is exposed to an untested drug
Explains that the dose starts very low because the safe and effective dose in people is not yet known, so a low dose limits the harm if the drug proves more toxic in humans than in animals

questions.modelAnswer: Developing a medicine goes through discovery, development, preclinical testing and then clinical testing, and each stage answers a question the previous one could not. Preclinical tests on cells, tissues and animals show whether the drug has an effect and give a first idea of its toxicity, but an animal is not a person, and a drug can behave differently in the human body. So the first clinical trials are about safety: does the drug cause harmful side effects in people? Healthy volunteers are used for this stage because they have no illness to confuse the picture: any change in them must be caused by the drug. It also means no patient who is already ill is exposed to a drug whose effects in people are unknown. The dose is kept very low to begin with and raised step by step. The dose that is safe, and the dose that is effective, have not yet been found in humans, and starting low limits the damage if the drug turns out to be more toxic than the animal tests suggested. Only once safety and a working dose range are known is the drug tested on patients with the infection to see whether it is effective.

questions.prompt:
A student spread one agar plate with bacteria and another with yeast, a fungus. On each plate she placed three paper discs of the same size: one soaked in an antibiotic, one in an antiseptic and one in sterile water. Every disc had a diameter of 6 mm. After incubation she measured the diameter of each clear zone, including the disc.

| Disc | Bacteria plate (mm) | Yeast plate (mm) |
|---|---|---|
| Antibiotic | 18 | 6 |
| Antiseptic | 14 | 13 |
| Sterile water | 6 | 6 |

Explain what these results show, and explain why the antibiotic gave a clear zone on one plate but not the other.
questions.skill: interpreting clear zones and why antibiotics act only on bacteria
questions.solution: A clear zone is agar where the microorganism **could not grow**, so its size shows how effective the substance is against that organism. The **sterile water** disc gave no zone beyond its own 6 mm on either plate, so the paper and the liquid themselves do not inhibit growth: any clear zone round the other discs is caused by the substance. The **antiseptic** gave zones on both plates (14 mm and 13 mm), so it kills or inhibits both bacteria and fungi. The **antibiotic** gave the largest zone on the bacteria plate (18 mm) but none at all on the yeast plate. Antibiotics work by **inhibiting cell processes in bacteria**, such as building the bacterial cell wall or making proteins on bacterial ribosomes; yeast is a fungus, and its cells do not have those bacterial processes, so the antibiotic has nothing to act on and the yeast grows right up to the disc. The comparison is fair because the discs were the same size and were incubated together on the same type of agar; repeating with more discs would show whether the difference between 14 mm and 13 mm is real.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): states that a clear zone means the microorganism did not grow and that the antibiotic worked on bacteria but not yeast, with little explanation

Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): uses the figures to compare the substances, identifies the water disc as a control, and explains that antibiotics act on bacteria only, but the reason in terms of bacterial cell processes or the antiseptic's broader action is incomplete

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a full account: clear zone as inhibited growth, the water disc showing the disc and liquid have no effect, the antiseptic inhibiting both organisms, and the antibiotic inhibiting cell processes found in bacteria but absent from fungal cells, so the yeast grows up to the disc

criteria.text: Explains that a clear zone is agar where the microorganism could not grow, so the diameter of the zone shows how effective a substance is against that organism
Explains that the sterile water disc is a control: no zone beyond the 6 mm disc on either plate shows the paper and liquid alone do not stop growth, so the other zones are due to the substances
States that the antiseptic produced a clear zone on both plates (14 mm and 13 mm), so it inhibits both bacteria and fungi
States that the antibiotic produced the largest zone on the bacteria plate (18 mm) but no zone on the yeast plate, so it inhibited the bacteria only
Explains that antibiotics inhibit cell processes found in bacteria, such as building the bacterial cell wall or making proteins on bacterial ribosomes
Explains that yeast is a fungus whose cells do not have those bacterial processes, so the antibiotic has nothing to act on and the yeast grew right up to the disc

questions.modelAnswer:
**Reading the plates.** After incubation each plate is covered with growth except where something stopped it. A clear zone is agar on which the microorganism could not grow, because the substance diffused out of the disc into the agar and killed the cells or stopped them dividing. The further it spread while still working, the larger the zone, so the diameter of the zone measures how effective the substance is against that organism.

**The control.** The sterile water disc gave no zone on either plate: the 6 mm measured is just the disc itself. This shows that the paper and the liquid on their own do not inhibit growth, so the clear zones round the other two discs must be caused by the antiseptic and the antibiotic.

**The antiseptic.** It gave a zone of 14 mm on the bacteria and 13 mm on the yeast. Antiseptics act on microorganisms in general, so it inhibited both the bacterium and the fungus, by about the same amount.

**The antibiotic.** On the bacteria plate it gave the largest zone of all, 18 mm, so it is the more effective of the two substances against this bacterium. On the yeast plate it gave no zone: the yeast grew right up to the edge of the disc. Antibiotics work by inhibiting cell processes that happen in bacteria, for example building the bacterial cell wall or making proteins on bacterial ribosomes, and that is also why they do not harm the cells of the person taking them. Yeast is a fungus. Its cells do not carry out those bacterial processes, so the antibiotic had nothing to act on and the yeast was unaffected. The result is the laboratory version of the rule that antibiotics treat bacterial infections only.

**How far to trust it.** The comparison is fair as far as it goes: the discs were the same size, so each carried a similar volume of liquid, and all three sat on the same agar for the same time at the same temperature. But there was only one disc of each substance per plate. Repeating with several discs, measuring two diameters at right angles on each zone and taking means would show whether the 14 mm and 13 mm zones are really different, and would stop one odd zone deciding the result.

examTechnique.body:
This topic mixes three kinds of question: recall of aseptic technique and the stages of drug development; calculation, where πr² appears and the radius must come from the diameter; and application, where monoclonal antibodies or a new antibiotic are placed in a context you have not seen. The core practical can be asked as a method to describe, a table to interpret or a conclusion to judge.

For calculations, write the radius on its own line before anything else, and give area units as mm². For conclusions from clear zones, compare areas, refer to the control, and do not stretch a result on one bacterium into a claim about all of them. For monoclonal antibodies, every use comes back to one idea: they bind to one specific antigen.
examinerErrors: Using the diameter in πr² instead of halving it first.
Giving antibiotics for a viral infection, or writing *antibodies* when *antibiotics* is meant.
Describing an aseptic technique without saying why it is used.
Leaving out the control disc, or concluding about all bacteria from one plate.
Saying hybridomas are made from two lymphocytes, or not saying why a tumour cell is needed.
Mixing up preclinical and clinical testing: preclinical is cells, tissues and animals; clinical is people.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer explains that antibiotics work by stopping a process that bacterial cells have and host cells do not, and uses that to reason about unfamiliar drugs. It calculates areas cleanly, halving the diameter and subtracting the disc where needed, and draws conclusions from clear zones that are limited to the bacterium tested. It describes hybridoma production by saying what each cell contributes, and explains every use of monoclonal antibodies through specific binding, including why targeted treatment harms fewer healthy cells than radiotherapy.
